Zomato doesn’t just create content.

It knows how to enter a moment people already care about.

That distinction matters.

Think about gully cricket.

You don’t need to explain why it matters to an Indian audience.

The rubber ball.
The makeshift stumps.
The neighbourhood.
The arguments.
The nostalgia.

Zomato’s recent Gully Cricket campaign understood that.

Instead of trying to manufacture attention, it stepped into an existing cultural conversation using real locations, raw street-cricket energy and familiar match-style storytelling. 0

That’s a much smarter marketing question:

Not:
“How do we get people to notice us?”

But:
“What are people already noticing?”

Because:

Context → relevance  
Relevance → attention  
Attention → conversation  
Conversation → recall

The best consumer brands don't always interrupt culture.

They understand it well enough to become part of it.

That’s what I find interesting about Zomato.

Not just the humour.

The timing.
The cultural fluency.
The understanding of everyday Indian behaviour.

And ultimately:

People may forget an ad.

They remember a brand that understood the moment.

What’s one Indian brand you think consistently understands its audience this well?

AI can create content in seconds.

But there’s one thing I still don’t trust it to understand on its own:

Why would a real person care?

I can ask AI for 50 hooks.
50 captions.
50 product ideas.
50 versions of the same campaign.

And technically, all 50 can be good.

But a consumer doesn’t stop scrolling because something is “good.”

They stop because something feels familiar.

A skincare ad works when it understands the insecurity behind the purchase.

A food-delivery app works when it understands the person ordering dinner at 11:30 PM after running on empty all day.

A productivity product works when it understands the guilt of having 17 things open and still feeling like nothing is done.

That’s where I think the real shift in marketing is happening.

AI is making content cheaper, faster and easier to produce.

So the scarce resource is no longer content.

It’s attention.

And even more importantly relevance.

Because people don’t remember everything a brand says.

They remember the one thing that made them think:

“Wait. That’s exactly me.”

That’s consumer psychology.

That’s product marketing.

And honestly, that’s the part of AI-powered marketing I find most interesting.

AI can generate the first layer.

Human understanding creates the reason to care.

The question I keep asking before I look at any piece of content is simple:

Would I stop?

Would I feel something?

Would I remember it tomorrow?

Because the future of marketing probably isn’t about who can create the most content.

It’s about who understands what deserves attention.

That’s the difference between creating content and creating relevance.

What’s one brand you think genuinely understands its consumer?

We’ve heard about the American Dream.

Work hard.
Build a career.
Buy a home.
Earn more.
Live on your own terms.

But somewhere along the way, the Indian Dream became something different.

Study hard → get a degree → get a job → get stable → support your family → and, if possible, leave.

The destination changes.

New York. London. Toronto. Dubai. Singapore.

But the underlying desire is often the same:

“I want a better life.”

And that made me wonder:

Why does success so often feel like an exit strategy?

Maybe the problem isn’t that Indians want to leave.

People should absolutely leave if they want to. 🌍

The real question is:

Why should building a good life here feel like the harder choice?

Because the next version of the Indian Dream shouldn’t simply be:

“How do I get out?”

It could be:

“How do we build a place worth staying for?”

Better products.
Better systems.
Better infrastructure.
Better opportunities.
Better companies.
Better everyday experiences.

Not because staying is morally superior.

But because choice is freedom.

Leave because you want to.
Stay because you want to.
Build because you believe it’s worth building.

That, to me, is a much more interesting definition of progress.

The dream is changing.

👇 Agree or disagree?

Tell me what YOUR Indian Dream looks like in one sentence.

#IndianDream #India #ConsumerBehaviour #Marketing #Culture #Business #FutureOfIndia #CreatorEconomy #KausshikaS

Bengaluru doesn’t just order food.

Sometimes, it orders back time.

It’s 9:30 PM.

You’ve been running since morning.
Meetings. Traffic. Deadlines. Messages.
Your laptop is still open.

And now you’re hungry.

But cooking feels like another deadline.

So you open Swiggy.

Not because you’re lazy.

Because sometimes, you’ve simply spent the entire day giving your energy to everything else.

And that tiny “Place Order” button suddenly gives you something more valuable than dinner:

30 minutes back.
An hour back.
A little breathing room.

That’s what makes convenience brands interesting to me.

People rarely buy the product alone.

They buy what the product gives them permission to do.

Swiggy isn’t only selling food in that moment.

It’s selling time.

Blinkit isn’t only selling groceries.

It’s selling immediacy.

And Zomato isn’t only selling a meal.

It’s selling an easier decision when your brain has already made 200 of them that day.

That’s consumer behaviour.

The product becomes valuable when it understands the moment behind the purchase.

And I think this is where brands become much more powerful.

Not when they convince people to buy more.

But when they understand **why people reach for them in the first place.**

Of course, convenience shouldn’t become a replacement for living.

Our bodies aren't machines.
We don't need to optimize every minute.
Some days, cooking is better.
Some days, walking to the store is better.
Some days, doing absolutely nothing is better.

But some nights?

Ordering dinner so you can finish your work, rest your mind, or simply breathe for a moment isn't laziness.

It’s a choice.

And sometimes, it’s a pretty rational one.

That’s the kind of consumer behaviour I love observing:

The tiny decisions we make every day —
and the brands quietly becoming part of those decisions.

So, Bengaluru…

What’s your 9:30 PM backup plan? 👀

Swiggy
